title: LangVersion, Target Framework Moniker (TFM), and breaking changes
hook: LangVersion controls which C# syntax the compiler accepts. The Target Framework Moniker (TFM) like net10.0 controls which runtime APIs exist. Upgrading either without a plan causes build breaks, nullable warnings, and package incompatibilities.

blocks.text: LangVersion can be latest, preview, or a specific number (14). TFM (net10.0, netstandard2.0) defines the API surface from reference assemblies. Breaking changes come from: nullable context on legacy code, removed APIs between .NET versions, stricter analyzers, and public API guards in shared libraries. Pin versions in Directory.Build.props for consistent CI builds.

blocks.text: A library on netstandard2.0 cannot use C# 12 features that require newer BCL types unless you multitarget. Turning on nullable on a million-line codebase floods warnings — migrate project by project. CI should catch TFM drift and unintended public API changes when you bump versions.

blocks.title: Upgrade order
blocks.body: Bump TFM first (fix API breaks), then enable nullable, then raise LangVersion for syntax sugar.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: LangVersion latest on library consumers cannot rebuild. Nullable enable everywhere in one PR. Upgrading TFM without running integration tests.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: pin LangVersion and TFM in Directory.Build.props — CI fails when a developer's local SDK defaults to latest syntax on an old TFM. ApiCompat and nullable analyzers in module 16 catch public API breaks before ship. Upgrading TFM runs integration tests; raising LangVersion alone does not add APIs. Breaking change playbook: TFM bump → fix API breaks → then adopt new syntax features incrementally.

snippet.label: Directory.Build.props — pin both axes
snippet.explanation: Line 4: LangVersion 14 legalizes syntax. Line 3: net10.0 selects BCL APIs. Mismatch — e.g. collection expressions on netstandard2.0 without polyfill — fails at compile or runtime.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying LangVersion and TFM are the same thing. Using latest LangVersion in a published NuGet without documenting required SDK. Nullable enable on legacy codebase in one PR without baseline. Adopting C# 14 extension syntax before TFM supports needed BCL types.

interviewTakeaways: LangVersion controls syntax; TFM controls available BCL APIs — two independent knobs.
Upgrade TFM first to fix API breaks; then raise LangVersion for new syntax.
Pin both in Directory.Build.props; ApiCompat and nullable analyzers catch breaks in CI.
60s: LangVersion syntax. TFM APIs. Pin in central props. TFM bump before syntax chase. Nullable incremental. latest in libraries hurts consumers.
Follow-up: can netstandard2.0 use C# 12 collection expressions?
commonPitfalls: Confusing LangVersion with TFM gets you rejected — syntax vs API availability.
Nullable enable everywhere in one PR on legacy code without baseline.
Strong answer: 'Directory.Build.props pins both. TFM upgrade first. LangVersion follows. ApiCompat on public API. Incremental nullable.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript target and lib mirror LangVersion plus TFM split — syntax vs available builtins.
Node engines pin runtime like TFM pins BCL. Babel/TS target pin syntax like LangVersion. Shipping a library without engines is like latest LangVersion — consumers on old runtimes break.
